title: US firm capacity is a size-stratified bundle of training, growth, infrastructure, and constraint
source_unit: World Bank Enterprise Survey country profile; 2,589 US establishments interviewed May 2024–April 2025

denominator.unit: interviewed US establishments; official country-profile sample

employment_growth_small.unit: percent; latest fiscal year relative to two years earlier

employment_growth_medium.unit: percent; latest fiscal year relative to two years earlier

employment_growth_large.unit: percent; latest fiscal year relative to two years earlier

observations.method: Official World Bank Enterprise Survey US country-profile table; establishment-size strata are reported separately and are not pooled into a synthetic firm-capacity score.
observations.uncertainty: The public country profile reports point values but not the full standard-error, variance, weighting, nonresponse, or common-universe documentation needed for a precision comparison here; employment growth is a reported survey measure, not a causal estimate.
observations.subgroup: Small (5–19 employees), medium (20–99), and large (100+) establishments.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher reported employment growth among large establishments may reflect composition, sector, age, sampling, or scale differences; it does not establish that large firms provide better jobs or greater worker control.

observations.period: 2024 survey fieldwork; training, infrastructure, and finance by establishment size

denominator.unit: interviewed US establishments; size-conditioned country-profile indicators

formal_training_small.unit: percent of small establishments offering formal training

formal_training_medium.unit: percent of medium establishments offering formal training

formal_training_large.unit: percent of large establishments offering formal training

electrical_outages_small.unit: percent of small establishments experiencing electrical outages

electrical_outages_medium.unit: percent of medium establishments experiencing electrical outages

electrical_outages_large.unit: percent of large establishments experiencing electrical outages

bank_financed_investment_small.unit: percent of small establishments using banks to finance investments

bank_financed_investment_medium.unit: percent of medium establishments using banks to finance investments

bank_financed_investment_large.unit: percent of large establishments using banks to finance investments

observations.method: Official World Bank Enterprise Survey country-profile indicators, shown by establishment size; each percentage retains its own indicator universe.
observations.uncertainty: The indicators are not a common firm-level panel and the public profile does not provide the complete variance surface; outage experience, training offer, and bank-finance use are separate measures.
observations.counterinterpretation: Large firms report both more formal training and more outage exposure; the pattern is compatible with greater infrastructure exposure or more complex operations, not simply greater capability or vulnerability.

observations.period: 2024 survey fieldwork; leading business obstacles by establishment size

inadequately_educated_workforce_small.unit: percent naming an inadequately educated workforce as the biggest obstacle; small establishments

tax_rates_small.unit: percent naming tax rates as the biggest obstacle; small establishments

labor_regulations_small.unit: percent naming labor regulations as the biggest obstacle; small establishments

observations.method: Top-obstacle question from the official country profile; respondents selected one biggest business-environment obstacle from the survey list.
observations.uncertainty: These are manager-reported perceptions, not independently verified constraints or causal effects; categories are mutually selected for the biggest-obstacle question but do not measure the intensity of all other obstacles.
observations.counterinterpretation: Small and large firms name different constraint mixes: workforce adequacy and tax rates are more prominent for small firms, while labor regulations are more prominent for large firms; this is not evidence that one size group faces less total constraint.

related_sources.claim: The World Bank released a separate US AI-focused follow-up survey in May 2026.
related_sources.access_boundary: The AI follow-up microdata and documentation remain behind the authenticated portal; this 2024 country profile is not an AI adoption estimate.

related_sources.claim: The public WBES indicator layer supports economy/subgroup indicators and can include standard errors and observation counts.
related_sources.access_boundary: The present record uses the official country-profile PDF values; it does not reconstruct a variance estimate from the public page.

boundary: This record establishes a bounded 2024 US firm baseline in which size is associated with different reported training, employment-growth, infrastructure, finance, and obstacle profiles. It does not estimate AI adoption, productivity causality, worker outcomes, firm survival, household incidence, or geopolitical leverage; the establishment survey size cells, indicator universes, and manager perceptions remain distinct evidence surfaces.
